A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same curvature-aware hyperbolic learning framework despite the changed title and expanded applications. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original LHIER metric-learning results, image-classification and VAE experiments, efficiency measurements, and component ablations in Appendix A.3.

after.justification: v3 retains original vision experiments and additionally reports HyperMAtt EEG results and metric-learning and EEG optimizer ablations in Appendix D.

M1.justification: Section 4.2 introduces HyperMAtt: SPD embeddings are projected into Lorentz space, SPD attention components are replaced with Lorentz counterparts, and classification uses a Lorentz MLR. This is a substantive architectural adaptation. The central curvature-transfer algorithm, Riemannian AdamW formulation, and distance-rescaling function are retained.

E1.justification: v3 adds EEG classification on MI, SSVEP, and ERN, covering motor imagery, visual stimuli, and error recognition beyond the earlier vision tasks. CIFAR-10 results disappear from the tables, but CIFAR-10 remains named in the setup, so discontinued evaluation is not established.

E2.justification: The new EEG comparison evaluates HyperMAtt against nine methods, including MAtt, EEGNet, EEG-TCNet, FBCNet, and ShallowConvNet. The transformer metric-learning comparison block is removed, and the ResNet-50 classification table drops the Hybrid Lorentz comparator. The retained CNN metric-learning comparator set is unchanged.

E3.justification: The new EEG evaluation adopts MAtt preprocessing and train/validation/test splits, uses fixed curvature, and evaluates accuracy for MI/SSVEP and AUC for ERN against collected published baseline scores. Reported metric-learning configurations are substantially narrowed by removing the DeiT, DINO, and ViT experiments. Existing vision settings are otherwise largely retained.

E4.justification: Appendix D adds LHIER comparisons across optimizers, constant curvature, and omission of the optimization scheme (Table 7), plus a HyperMAtt optimizer ablation (Table 8). These directly examine component contributions beyond the retained image-classification ablation, which moves from v2 Table 5 to v3 Table 6 without numerical changes.

E5.justification: Section 4.2 newly specifies three runs with means and standard deviations for HyperMAtt. The retained ResNet-18 and VAE experiments still report five runs. This adds replication information for the new experiments without establishing increased replication of existing results.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces LHIER ResNet-50 R@1 values for CUB/Cars/SOP of 72.4/89.1/81.3 with 73.4/90.0/81.9; these are revised reported results, not an established controlled performance gain. EEG results and optimizer ablations are added, while transformer and CIFAR-10 entries are removed. HyperMAtt leads the reported SSVEP and ERN comparisons but not MI. Matched retained classification and VAE values are unchanged.

T1.justification: v3 adds an explicit Lorentz inner-product bound and an inverse-hyperbolic-cosine domain argument in Sections 3.1–3.2. It removes the explicit Stiefel-manifold definition and Cayley-based mathematical justification from the convolution discussion. The curvature-transfer norm identity and appendix scaling derivation are retained.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction broaden the contribution from stable, efficient hyperbolic vision learning to improved generalization and resistance to overfitting, explicitly include EEG, and claim state-of-the-art performance in two domains. The contribution list now foregrounds domain adaptations, including HyperMAtt, while retaining the optimizer and rescaling claims.

C2.justification: v3 introduces data-scarcity and overfitting explanations for AdamW, and explicitly avoids EEG curvature learning because it could worsen overfitting. It removes v2's discussion of limited transformer gains, architectural or tuning explanations, batch-normalization bottlenecks, and limitations of norm-matching dimensionality reduction. These materially change applicability qualifications and interpretation.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies Lorentz layer normalization and rescaling placements for LHIER. Conversely, the explicit Cayley construction and Lorentz-Core bottleneck recipe are no longer fully documented, although convolution pseudocode and bottleneck references remain. A new code-availability statement contains a redacted placeholder rather than usable access information.

R1.justification: Research positioning expands into EEG manifold attention and data-scarce generalization, adding MAtt, EEG baseline and dataset literature, and supporting overfitting references. The dedicated metric-learning related-work discussion and numerous metric-learning citations are removed. The central positioning against GeoOpt curvature updates and earlier hyperbolic CNNs remains.

P1.justification: The introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten, optimizer topics become separate subsections, and experiments are reorganized as domain adaptations with repeated problem-setting, adaptation, and experimental-goal headings. Convolution material moves to Appendix B, appendices are reorganized, and an impact statement is added. The title and author list also change.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column main layout and substantially restructures the tables, removing transformer blocks and several metric or dataset columns while adding EEG and optimizer-ablation tables. The Lorentz-Core bottleneck diagram is removed. The tangent-plane and scaling figures are retained with relocation, resizing, or relabeling.

improvement.justification: The new metric-learning and EEG optimizer ablations provide useful component-level evidence, and HyperMAtt extends validation beyond vision. However, v3 removes extensive transformer comparisons, including unfavorable outcomes, and drops substantive limitations and implementation explanations while strengthening its generalization and state-of-the-art claims. The gains in validation coexist with reduced transparency about architecture dependence and remaining weaknesses, preventing a reliable net judgment of overall quality.
